passages.title: The Environmental Cost of Consumer Goods
passages.subtitle: How mass production, packaging, and throwaway habits leave a heavy footprint
paragraphs: Walk into any modern shopping mall or open a shopping app, and you can buy cheap clothes, phones, and kitchen gadgets in seconds. This culture of constant buying is known as consumerism. Thanks to modern mass production in giant factories, items that once took days to make by hand are now produced in millions at very low prices.

However, cheap shopping carries a hidden price for nature. Every product has a carbon footprint—the total amount of greenhouse gases released when making, shipping, and throwing it away. For instance, fast-fashion brands use huge amounts of water and chemical dyes to make trendy T-shirts that shoppers may wear only a few times before throwing out.

Another major problem is disposable products and unnecessary packaging. Coffee cups, plastic cutlery, and takeaway boxes are often used for just ten minutes, yet they can sit in rubbish dumps for hundreds of years. Online shopping has also increased waste, as small items are frequently wrapped in layers of bubble wrap and oversized cardboard boxes.

Even expensive electronics do not always last long. Some manufacturers practise planned obsolescence—designing phones, printers, or washing machines so they break down or become slow after only two or three years, forcing customers to buy brand-new models. Repairing an old device is often made difficult because spare parts are costly or batteries are glued shut.

Fortunately, a growing movement toward ethical consumption is fighting back. More shoppers are choosing second-hand clothes, bringing reusable coffee mugs, and visiting local 'repair cafes' where volunteers fix broken toasters and laptops for free. Several European countries have also passed 'right-to-repair' laws requiring electronics firms to supply spare parts for up to ten years.

passages.title: From Fossil Fuels to Renewable Energy
passages.subtitle: The benefits and practical challenges of switching to solar and wind power
paragraphs: A For over two hundred years, modern civilisation has run mainly on fossil fuels—coal, oil, and natural gas. Because these fuels took millions of years to form underground, they are non-renewable and will eventually run low. More urgently, burning them creates air pollution and drives global warming, pushing countries to shift quickly toward renewable energy.

B Among clean options, solar and wind power have grown the fastest. Unlike coal power stations, solar panels and wind turbines produce electricity without releasing carbon dioxide or smoky fumes. Once built, sunlight and wind are free, meaning clean power plants have very low daily running costs and can supply electricity for decades.

C Switching to renewables also improves national energy security. Many nations currently buy oil and gas from foreign countries, leaving drivers and factories vulnerable whenever global fuel prices jump suddenly. Generating electricity from local sunshine and coastal winds helps governments reduce dependence on imported fuels and keeps household energy bills steadier over time.

D Despite these clear advantages, moving away from fossil fuels faces two big practical challenges. First, building large wind farms, solar fields, and new power lines requires a very high initial investment. Second, renewable power depends heavily on the weather: solar panels stop making power at night, and wind turbines slow down on calm days, so countries still struggle to keep lights on twenty-four hours a day.

E Engineers are working hard to solve these limits. Giant lithium and sand batteries are now being built to store extra electricity generated on sunny or windy afternoons for use during dark winter evenings. In addition, linking national power grids across neighbouring countries allows a windy region to share spare power with a calm one.

F Prices for solar panels have already fallen by more than eighty percent over the last fifteen years. With continued research, government support, and smarter storage systems, experts believe renewable energy can soon become both the cleanest and the cheapest way to power the world.

passages.title: Oil and Gas in Untouched Wilderness
passages.subtitle: Should energy companies be allowed to drill in the planet's last wild places?
paragraphs: 1 As the world's population grows and economies expand, global energy demand remains very high. Because many old oil fields are slowly running dry, energy companies are looking toward remote regions—such as the Arctic tundra, deep rainforests, and icy polar seas—for new reserves. This push has sparked fierce debate over whether drilling should ever be permitted in an untouched wilderness.

2 Supporters of resource extraction argue that opening remote oil and gas fields brings clear economic gains. Developing new supplies can keep petrol and heating costs affordable for ordinary families and create thousands of well-paid engineering jobs in poor or isolated towns. Energy firms also claim that modern computers and safer pipes make drilling much cleaner than it was fifty years ago.

3 Environmental scientists strongly disagree. Even before a single drop of oil is pumped, building roads, pipelines, and landing strips slices through a pristine environment. Heavy trucks and noisy machinery cause serious habitat destruction, scaring away migrating reindeer, polar bears, and rare forest birds that depend on quiet, unbroken land to raise their young.

4 An even greater fear is a major oil spill. In freezing Arctic waters or dense tropical jungles, rough weather and long distances from rescue ports make accidents extremely hard to clean up. A single leaking pipe can poison rivers, coat seabirds in thick black oil, and leave lasting ecological damage that takes decades to heal—destroying local fishing and hunting communities along the way.

5 Indigenous groups who have lived in these wild areas for centuries often voice the strongest opposition. For them, forests and rivers are not empty wasteland waiting to be mined; they are living homes that provide food, clean water, and cultural identity. Many argue that short-term profits go mainly to distant corporations while local residents are left with polluted water.

6 In my view, drilling in the Earth's last wild corners is a dangerous step backwards. Instead of spending billions searching for hard-to-reach oil that worsens climate change, governments and energy companies should direct that money toward renewable power and energy efficiency. Once a pristine wilderness is lost, no amount of money can bring it back.
